passage.title: The Unpainted Archway
passage.author: BEACON Assessment Lab
passage.text:
High on the wood scaffold outside the brick hall, young Mateo held his soft brush. He dipped the tip into a jar of warm gold paint. Forty years ago, the town's famous muralist, Elena Soto, had painted a grand fresco across three walls of the courtyard. The artwork showed the history of the valley, from early cedar canoes to busy train depots. Over the decades, summer sun and winter rain had dulled the once vibrant colors beneath a layer of gray street dust. Now Mateo was helping the town art guild restore the mural before the autumn festival.

Mateo worked slowly along the west wall so he would not scratch the dry lime plaster. The faded cobalt river, bordered by rows of brick mill houses, was gently cleaned by Mateo with a damp sponge and warm chalk water. As the gray soot washed away, rich blue waves and bright copper roofs gleamed in the morning light once more. Yet whenever Mateo glanced toward the fourth wall on the east side of the arch, a puzzle bothered him. That wide plaster panel was completely blank, save for a painted stone archway at the very edge.

At first, Mateo assumed that Elena Soto had run out of grant money or fallen ill before she could finish the east panel. During his lunch break, he opened a crate of Soto's old sketchbooks stored in the library basement. To his surprise, the books held finished charcoal plans for the first three walls. Yet not a single page showed a sketch for the fourth. Instead, taped inside the back cover, he found a short letter Soto had written to the town council in 1984.

Squinting in the dim basement light, Mateo read her neat script closely to discern her true purpose. In the letter, Soto explained that the blank east wall was a deliberate choice, not an accident. She wrote that a neighborhood's story never ends with its past, so she had painted an open stone archway leading onto bare white plaster. She wanted future young artists of the valley to paint their own chapter when their time came.

Climbing back up the scaffold that afternoon, Mateo looked at the empty white wall with fresh eyes. He realized that restoring the old fresco was only half of the task Elena Soto had left behind. He called down to the guild leader below. Then he held up the 1984 letter and pointed to the bare arch. The blank plaster was not a flaw to hide, but a living legacy waiting for his generation's brush.

tier2Words.definition: Bright, rich, and full of lively energy or color
tier2Words.rootHint: vibr- (Latin root meaning 'to shake' or 'pulse with life')
tier2Words.contextClue: Contrasted with how sun and rain 'had dulled' the colors beneath gray street dust.

tier2Words.definition: To recognize, make out, or understand something clearly
tier2Words.rootHint: dis- + cern (Latin root meaning 'to sift' or 'separate')

tier2Words.definition: Done intentionally and on purpose after careful thought
tier2Words.rootHint: de- + libr (Latin root meaning 'to weigh in a balance')

tier2Words.rootHint: leg- (Latin root meaning 'to send as a gift or bequest')

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The faded cobalt river, bordered by rows of brick mill houses, was gently cleaned by Mateo with a damp sponge and warm chalk water."

Who or what performed the action of cleaning in this sentence?

options.text: The rows of brick mill houses along the border
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the first 'by' phrase inside the participial modifier ('bordered by rows of brick mill houses') with the actor of the main verb.
options.childFeedback: The rows of brick mill houses are part of the painted picture bordering the river on the wall; painted houses cannot clean anything!

options.text: Mateo, using a damp sponge and warm chalk water
options.diagnosticNote: Correctly identifies 'by Mateo' as the agent performing the passive verb 'was gently cleaned'.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'was gently cleaned by Mateo with a damp sponge and warm chalk water' shows that Mateo performed the action of cleaning the painted river.

options.text: The faded cobalt river painted on the west wall
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the grammatical subject/receiver of the cleaning ('The faded cobalt river') with the actor.
options.childFeedback: The faded cobalt river is the painted part of the mural that received the cleaning, not the person holding the damp sponge.

options.text: Elena Soto, the town's famous muralist from forty years ago
options.diagnosticNote: Imports Elena Soto from Paragraph 1 even though she is not mentioned in this sentence.
options.childFeedback: Elena Soto painted the mural forty years ago (Paragraph 1), whereas young Mateo is the one cleaning it in Paragraph 2.

questions.provingSentenceText: The faded cobalt river, bordered by rows of brick mill houses, was gently cleaned by Mateo with a damp sponge and warm chalk water.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'was gently cleaned by Mateo with a damp sponge and warm chalk water' shows that Mateo performed the action of cleaning the painted river.
questions.parentExplanation: Sentence Surgery item (ELAGSE5L1). Like many 1080L sentences, this sentence contains a distractor 'by' phrase inside an embedded modifier ('bordered by rows of brick mill houses') before the main passive verb ('was gently cleaned by Mateo').
questions.retryHint: Look at the words right after 'cleaned by' in the Paragraph 2 sentence to see who washed the soot off the mural.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"In the letter, Soto explained that the blank east wall was a deliberate choice, not an accident."

What does the word deliberate most likely mean as it is used in the sentence?

options.text: Careless and forgotten during a busy project
options.diagnosticNote: Selects an antonym that contradicts the contrast clue 'not an accident.'
options.childFeedback: The sentence explicitly says 'not an accident,' so 'deliberate' is the exact opposite of careless or forgotten.

options.text: Covered in thick layers of gray street dust
options.diagnosticNote: Borrows descriptive language from Paragraph 1 unrelated to the meaning of 'deliberate.'
options.childFeedback: Gray street dust covered the painted walls in Paragraph 1, whereas 'deliberate' in Paragraph 4 describes Soto's purposeful choice to leave the east wall blank.

options.text: Planned on purpose with a clear goal in mind
options.diagnosticNote: Uses the direct contrast clue ('not an accident') and Paragraph 4's explanation of her goal for future artists.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'deliberate' means planned on purpose with a clear goal in mind, which the sentence directly contrasts with 'not an accident.'

options.text: Too expensive for the town council to afford
options.diagnosticNote: Repeats Mateo's mistaken first guess from Paragraph 3 ('run out of grant money') which the letter disproves.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, Mateo first guessed Soto had run out of grant money, but Paragraph 4 proves she left the wall blank on purpose for future artists.

questions.provingSentenceText: In the letter, Soto explained that the blank east wall was a deliberate choice, not an accident.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'deliberate' means planned on purpose with a clear goal in mind, which the sentence directly contrasts with 'not an accident.'
questions.parentExplanation: Contextual vocabulary item (ELAGSE5L4). The author provides an explicit contrast clue ('a deliberate choice, not an accident'), proving that 'deliberate' means intentional or planned on purpose.
questions.retryHint: Notice the contrast clue right at the end of the sentence in Paragraph 4 ('a deliberate choice, not an accident').

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraphs 3 and 4, how did Mateo's understanding of the blank east wall change after he searched the library basement?

options.text: He realized that the town council had painted white plaster over Elena Soto's original charcoal drawings.
options.diagnosticNote: Misinterprets the text; Soto never drew a plan for the fourth wall and left it bare herself.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 states that Soto's sketchbooks had zero sketches for the fourth wall, because she never drew or painted scenes on that wall in the first place.

options.text: He discovered that Elena Soto had intentionally left the wall blank as an invitation for future young artists to paint their own chapter.
options.diagnosticNote: Accurately contrasts his initial assumption (illness or lack of money) with the truth revealed in the 1984 letter.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, Mateo first thought Soto ran out of money or fell ill, but her 1984 letter in Paragraph 4 revealed she left the wall blank on purpose so future young artists could paint their own chapter.

options.text: He learned that the lime plaster on the east wall was too cracked and damp to hold gold or cobalt paint.
options.diagnosticNote: Invents a structural flaw in the east wall plaster not supported by the passage.
options.childFeedback: The letter never says the lime plaster on the east wall was cracked or damp; Soto left the bare white plaster ready for future brushes.

options.text: He decided that no artist should ever touch the east wall so it would stay completely white forever.
options.diagnosticNote: Uses extreme words ('no artist should ever', 'forever') that reverse Soto's wish for young artists to paint it.
options.childFeedback: Instead of wanting the wall to stay white forever, Soto wrote that she wanted future young artists of the valley to paint their own chapter on it.

questions.provingSentenceText: She wanted future young artists of the valley to paint their own chapter when their time came.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, Mateo first thought Soto ran out of money or fell ill, but her 1984 letter in Paragraph 4 revealed she left the wall blank on purpose so future young artists could paint their own chapter.
questions.parentExplanation: Click-to-Prove Inference item (ELAGSE5RL1). In Paragraph 3, Mateo initially assumes Soto ran out of funds or fell ill; in Paragraph 4, her 1984 letter reveals she left the wall open so future young artists could add their own chapter.
questions.retryHint: Compare what Mateo first guessed at the start of Paragraph 3 with what Elena Soto's 1984 letter explained in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Why does the author include the symbol of the 'painted stone archway at the very edge' of the blank wall in Paragraphs 2 and 4?

options.text: To show that Elena Soto only knew how to paint stone buildings and could not paint trees or rivers
options.diagnosticNote: Uses 'only' and contradicts Paragraphs 1 and 2, which describe her painting cedar canoes and a cobalt river.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 1 and 2 show that Soto painted cedar canoes and a cobalt river, proving she could paint much more than just stone buildings.

options.text: To mark the exact spot where builders planned to knock down the brick library wall to add a new door
options.diagnosticNote: Takes the painted archway literally as a construction blueprint rather than part of the mural.
options.childFeedback: The archway was painted on the courtyard wall as a symbol in the mural, not as a construction mark for knocking down a brick library wall.

options.text: To visually connect the valley's past on the first three walls with an open doorway leading into the community's future
options.diagnosticNote: Captures the symbolic structural role of the archway as a bridge from the historical scenes into the unfinished future.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, Elena Soto explains that because a neighborhood's story never ends with its past, the painted stone archway acts as an open doorway leading from the valley's history into its future.

options.text: To prove that the art guild had already finished painting the fourth wall before Mateo arrived
options.diagnosticNote: Contradicts the passage, which states that the fourth wall was completely blank except for the archway edge.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 clearly states that the fourth wall on the east side was completely blank except for the painted archway at the edge.

questions.provingSentenceText: She wrote that a neighborhood's story never ends with its past, so she had painted an open stone archway leading onto bare white plaster.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, Elena Soto explains that because a neighborhood's story never ends with its past, the painted stone archway acts as an open doorway leading from the valley's history into its future.
questions.parentExplanation: Craft & Structure item (ELAGSE5RL5). The painted stone archway functions both as the mystery hook in Paragraph 2 and the thematic bridge in Paragraph 4 connecting the valley's past to its unfinished future.
questions.retryHint: Read the third and fourth sentences of Paragraph 4 to see why Soto painted an open stone archway leading onto the bare white plaster.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the passage?

options.text: Honoring a community's heritage means not only preserving its past, but also adding new chapters for the future.
options.diagnosticNote: Synthesizes Mateo's restoration of the old fresco (preserving the past) with his realization that his generation is meant to paint the fourth wall (adding the future).
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, Mateo realizes that restoring the old fresco is only half the task—honoring Elena Soto's legacy also means picking up the brush to paint his generation's new chapter.

options.text: Warm chalk water and soft sponges are the only safe supplies for cleaning forty-year-old outdoor murals.
options.diagnosticNote: Focuses on a minor restoration technique from Paragraph 2 and adds the extreme word 'only.'
options.childFeedback: How Mateo cleans the west wall with a sponge and chalk water in Paragraph 2 is a small craft detail, not the big message of the story.

options.text: Old sketchbooks should always be locked away in basements so young artists do not copy earlier styles.
options.diagnosticNote: Contradicts the story, where reading the old sketchbook letter inspires Mateo and reveals Soto's invitation.
options.childFeedback: Finding the sketchbook crate in the library basement helped Mateo discover Soto's letter; the story never says sketchbooks should be locked away.

options.text: Artists who start large public projects rarely finish their work on time for autumn festivals.
options.diagnosticNote: Misinterprets the deliberate blank wall as procrastination.
options.childFeedback: Elena Soto did not fail to finish her project on time—Paragraph 4 proves that leaving the fourth wall blank was her deliberate artistic plan.

questions.provingSentenceText: The blank plaster was not a flaw to hide, but a living legacy waiting for his generation's brush.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 5, Mateo realizes that restoring the old fresco is only half the task—honoring Elena Soto's legacy also means picking up the brush to paint his generation's new chapter.
questions.parentExplanation: Focus standard ELAGSE5RL2 (Theme). The passage builds to the insight in Paragraphs 4 and 5 that a community's story is an ongoing legacy: honoring the past includes contributing the next chapter.
questions.retryHint: Read Paragraph 5 to see how Mateo connects restoring the old mural with what his generation is meant to do on the blank plaster.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Over the decades, summer sun and winter rain had dulled the once vibrant colors beneath a layer of gray street dust."
options.diagnosticNote: Explains why the mural needed cleaning in Paragraph 1, but does not capture the theme of adding new chapters.
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 only explains how weather dulled the old paint over time, without mentioning the future chapter on the blank wall.

options.text: "At first, Mateo assumed that Elena Soto had run out of grant money or fallen ill before she could finish the east panel."
options.diagnosticNote: Quotes Mateo's initial mistaken assumption before he discovers the true meaning of the blank wall.
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 3 states Mateo's mistaken first guess before he read Elena Soto's letter and learned the true meaning of the blank wall.

options.text: "During his lunch break, he opened a crate of Soto's old sketchbooks stored in the library basement."
options.diagnosticNote: Describes a plot action in Paragraph 3 without stating the thematic message.
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 3 just shows Mateo opening the crate at lunch, before he discovers the letter or understands the theme.

options.text: "The blank plaster was not a flaw to hide, but a living legacy waiting for his generation's brush."
options.diagnosticNote: Directly proves the theme in Part A by framing the unfinished wall as a living legacy for the new generation to continue.
options.childFeedback: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly captures the theme in Question 5 by calling the blank wall a 'living legacy waiting for his generation's brush.'

questions.provingSentenceText: The blank plaster was not a flaw to hide, but a living legacy waiting for his generation's brush.
questions.childTip: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly captures the theme in Question 5 by calling the blank wall a 'living legacy waiting for his generation's brush.'
questions.parentExplanation: Part B requires selecting the verbatim quote in Paragraph 5 that directly proves the theme of continuing a community's artistic legacy.
